epithet: Mu'adhdhin al-Rasul (Caller to Prayer of the Messenger ﷺ); Sayyidna Bilal
tribe: Non-Arab origin — Abyssinian (Ethiopian); enslaved by Banu Jumah of Quraysh
role: First Mu'adhdhin (Caller to Prayer) of Islam
Early Convert and Champion of Monotheism
summary: Bilal ibn Rabah (RA) was an Abyssinian slave who became one of the earliest Muslims and one of the most celebrated figures in Islamic history. His steadfast refusal to recant his faith under brutal torture, his rescue by Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, and his appointment as the first Mu'adhdhin (caller to prayer) of Islam make him a symbol of human dignity, perseverance, and the universal brotherhood that Islam proclaimed.
biography:
Bilal ibn Rabah al-Habashi was born around 580 CE in Makkah. His mother Hamamah was an Abyssinian slave, and his father Rabah was likely also enslaved, making Bilal a slave by birth under the customs of pre-Islamic Arabian society. He was owned by Umayyah ibn Khalaf, a prominent and cruel man of the Banu Jumah clan of Quraysh who was among the fiercest opponents of Islam.

Bilal accepted Islam in the earliest days of the Prophet's mission, at a time when only a small handful of people had embraced the new faith. His conversion was a matter of heart and conviction, not social calculation — for a slave to accept the religion of a man opposed by the most powerful people in Makkah was an act of extraordinary courage. When his master Umayyah ibn Khalaf learned of his conversion, he subjected Bilal to some of the most severe torture recorded from the early Makkan period.

The narrations in al-Tabaqat al-Kubra (Ibn Sa'd, Vol. 3) and Ibn Hisham's al-Seerah al-Nabawiyyah describe his torture in detail: he was taken to the scorching desert outside Makkah during the midday heat, stripped, laid flat on the burning gravel, and had a heavy boulder placed on his chest to prevent him from moving. He was flogged repeatedly and given no water. Umayyah and his associates demanded that he renounce Islam and acknowledge their gods Lat and Uzza. Bilal's response, in the face of this treatment, was singular and defiant: 'Ahad, Ahad!' — 'One! One!' — affirming the oneness of Allah with every blow. This response, which he repeated no matter what was done to him, became one of the most celebrated declarations of tawhid in Islamic history.

Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (RA) passed by during one of these sessions of torture and, moved by what he witnessed, negotiated with Umayyah ibn Khalaf for Bilal's manumission. He paid a significant sum — various classical narrations differ on the amount, ranging from five to nine uqiyyah of gold — to purchase and immediately free Bilal. The Prophet ﷺ said of this: 'Abu Bakr, he is our brother.' Umayyah mockingly said that he would have sold him for even less, to which Abu Bakr replied that he would have bought him for far more. (Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra, Vol. 3; also referenced in Sahih al-Bukhari in the context of Bilal's virtues)

After the Hijrah to Madinah, when the time came to establish the call to prayer, the Prophet ﷺ was advised by Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA) — who had seen in a dream a man being taught the words of the adhan — about its form. The Prophet ﷺ chose Bilal to be the first person in history to call the adhan, appointing him as Mu'adhdhin of Islam. His powerful and resonant voice rang out over Madinah with the words that would echo across the Muslim world for all of time: 'Allahu Akbar...' (Sunan Abi Dawud, Kitab al-Salah; al-Tirmidhi, Kitab al-Salah; Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra)

Bilal served as the personal Mu'adhdhin of the Prophet ﷺ throughout his life in Madinah. He was also a trusted companion in many other capacities: he served as the Prophet's steward and aide in certain administrative matters, guarded his belongings, and carried his personal equipment on campaigns. He participated in all major military engagements including Badr, Uhud, and the conquest of Makkah.

At the Conquest of Makkah (8 AH / 630 CE), one of the most symbolically resonant moments of the event occurred when Bilal climbed to the top of the Ka'bah — the sacred house itself — and called the adhan from there. This act, which would have been unthinkable in the social hierarchy of pre-Islamic Makkah where he had been a tortured slave, was a statement about the nature of the Islam that had just prevailed: that honor before Allah was based on taqwa (God-consciousness), not lineage, race, or social standing. The Quraysh present who had not yet embraced Islam were reportedly stunned.

When the Prophet ﷺ died in 11 AH (632 CE), Bilal was overcome with grief. He reportedly called the adhan only once after the Prophet's death — on the day of his funeral — and broke down weeping before he could complete it, unable to say the words 'Ashhadu anna Muhammadan Rasulullah' without being overcome. He never called the adhan again in Madinah after that, unable to bear the absence of the one who had first appointed him. He left Madinah and traveled to Syria (Sham) to participate in the military campaigns there under Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah.

There is a narration — recorded by al-Dhahabi in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala' and referenced in classical Seerah literature — that Umar ibn al-Khattab, when he later visited Syria and met Bilal, asked him to call the adhan one final time. Bilal agreed, and the Sahaba present wept intensely, remembering the Prophet ﷺ.

Bilal died around 20 AH (641 CE) in Damascus, Syria, reportedly at approximately sixty years of age. He was buried in Damascus, where his grave is traditionally identified. The Prophet ﷺ had honored him as a companion of paradise — telling him after the conquest of Makkah: 'Tell me the most hopeful deed you have done, O Bilal, for I heard the sound of your sandals in Paradise ahead of me.' Bilal replied: 'There is nothing I consider more hopeful than that whenever I make wudu at any hour of the day or night, I pray as many rak'ah as Allah wills.' (Sahih al-Bukhari, Kitab Tahajjud)

Bilal's life stands as one of the most powerful illustrations of Islam's revolutionary social ethic — a man who was tortured as a slave for his monotheism became the voice that called the entire Muslim world to prayer. Classical scholars universally regard him among the most beloved companions of the Prophet ﷺ and a figure whose story belongs to the entire ummah.

key_events.event: Accepted Islam among the earliest converts in Makkah
Tortured by Umayyah ibn Khalaf; responded with 'Ahad, Ahad!'
Purchased and freed by Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (RA)
Emigrated to Madinah with the Hijrah
Appointed first Mu'adhdhin of Islam; called the first adhan in Madinah
Fought in the Battle of Badr; killed his former tormentor Umayyah ibn Khalaf in the aftermath
Climbed atop the Ka'bah to call the adhan at the Conquest of Makkah
Called the adhan at the Prophet's funeral; wept and could not continue; left Madinah

notable_traits: Unbreakable faith under severe physical torture — his 'Ahad! Ahad!' became a symbol of tawhid
Powerful, resonant voice that the Prophet ﷺ chose above all others for the adhan
Deep love and loyalty to the Prophet ﷺ — could not bear to call the adhan after his death
Living symbol of Islam's rejection of racial and social hierarchy
Humility and gratitude in the exercise of a role of great spiritual significance

key_relationships.spouse: A woman from the Banu Zuhrah tribe (name not consistently recorded in classical sources)
